stem: A single circuit is wrapped in a batch to cut its queuing time. Why does this not help?

options.text: A batch always dispatches the wrapped single circuit to a simulator for validation first, so it never waits in the queue.
Batches only speed up circuits with more than 100 gates.
The batch usually cancels a lone job, because a batch requires at least two jobs to schedule.
The queuing time does not decrease for the first job in a batch, so a single circuit gains nothing from one.
The queuing time actually doubles, because the batch itself has to be scheduled before any of its jobs can enter the queue.
It does help, but only marginally — the batch's parallel classical processing usually shaves the transpilation off the critical path.

explanation.correct: Batching helps by scheduling multiple jobs together and parallelizing their classical processing. But the first job in a batch still waits in the normal queue, so a batch (or session) provides no benefit when there is only one job.

distractors.A: Nothing validates a batch on a simulator first; the execution target is set by the mode/backend, and the job queues on the QPU exactly as it would in job mode.
distractors.B: Batch benefits come from parallel scheduling across jobs, not from circuit size; there is no gate-count threshold.
distractors.C: A batch does not require or enforce a minimum of two jobs, and it never cancels a lone job.
distractors.E: A batch is not queued ahead of its jobs, and it adds no queue of its own. The point is simply that the first job still enters the normal queue and waits exactly as long as it would on its own.
distractors.F: The guide's "classical computation, such as compilation, is run in parallel" is about the service-side processing of several submitted jobs side by side; your own transpilation happens locally before submission. With one job there is nothing to overlap it with, so a lone batched circuit gains nothing.
